title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarking & runbooks
author: Daniel Kim
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, release notes highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers owning the runtime, SREs, and solutions engineers who onboard customers to Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments.

Sections:
  - Architecture overview
  - Kernel scheduling strategies and policies
  - Profiling playbook (how-to, tools, metrics)
  - Benchmarking suite (benchmarks, commands, baselines)
  - Recent release notes (summary)
  - Known issues & workarounds
  - Runtime runbooks & incident procedures
  - Team wiki & ownership

Purpose and scope:
  - Single-source reference for runtime operational practices and design rationale.
  - Covers both hosted and private deployment modes unless explicitly called out.
  - Assumes familiarity with container orchestration, GPU concepts, and model serving basics.

1) Architecture overview

High-level components:
  - Frontend Router (api-gateway): handles authentication, rate limiting, per-customer quotas and routes to appropriate pool.
  - Request Router (router-service): policy-based routing (latency vs cost vs region).
  - Batcher (batch-service): groups requests for efficient GPU utilization while honoring latency SLOs.
  - Scheduler / Kernel Selector (scheduler-service): chooses execution kernel variant (FP32/FP16/INT8; fused kernels) and assigns to GPU devices.
  - KV Cache (kv-cache-service): prefix/KV caching across requests and model variants; supports per-tenant and global caches.
  - Worker (inference-worker): runtime binary that runs kernels, manages KV cache locally, exposes metrics, and serves streamed tokens.
  - Telemetry & Tracing (observability): Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and per-request token cost accounting.

Design goals and constraints:
  - Latency SLOs: 99th percentile tail < 200ms for short-chat requests (<=128 tokens) on Dedicated small class; 95th percentile < 1500ms for long generations depending on sequence length.
  - Throughput: Support bursty PLG traffic via autoscaling and continuous batching.
  - Cost control: use kernel selection, quantization profiles and cache reuse to minimize per-token cost.
  - Isolation: Strong tenant isolation for Dedicated and Private via cgroups, GPU MIG where available, and network namespaces.

Deployment topologies:
  - Hosted: shared control plane, per-tenant logical pools, optimistic scheduling.
  - Dedicated: reserved GPU pools with strict quota enforcement and non-preemptive scheduling for committed customers.
  - Private: customer-managed control plane; our operator handles orchestration and runtime binaries with constrained privileges.

2) Kernel scheduling strategies and policies

Objective: maximize GPU throughput without violating latency SLOs and tenant isolation.

Policy types (configurable by pool):
  - Latency-first (default for low-latency customers): enforce small batch sizes, preemptible background work, priority queues for real-time requests.
  - Throughput-first (batching-heavy): allow larger max batch sizes, higher queue time budget, favor kernel variants with higher throughput (e.g., fused attention kernels).
  - Cost-optimized: prefer INT8/quantized kernels and CPU fallback for low-priority jobs.

Key scheduling primitives:
  - Priority queues: real-time (P0), interactive (P1), background (P2).
  - Timeouts / queue budgets: per-priority max queue delay (e.g., P0 <= 10ms, P1 <= 50ms, P2 <= 200ms).
  - Affinity: prefer colocated KV cache and model weights for warmed workers to reduce cold-start.
  - Preemption: background jobs are preemptible by higher-priority work where hardware supports context switching; preemption is disabled for Dedicated reserved workloads by default.
  - Kernel selection rules: match model architecture, sequence length bucket, and requested quality profile to choose kernel variant.

Scheduling knobs exposed in pool config (example table):

| config_field | description | example |
|--------------|-------------|---------|
| max_batch_size | upper bound on aggregated tokens for a batch | 2048 |
| max_queue_ms | max time to wait to form a batch | 50 |
| priority_weights | relative weight for priority classes | {P0:10,P1:5,P2:1} |
| kernel_policy | ordered list of kernel candidates with fallback | [fp16_fused, fp16, int8] |
| preemption | boolean, whether background jobs can be preempted | true |

Note: the above table is illustrative. Actual pool configs are stored as YAML in infra repo (see related_pages).

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

When to profile:
  - New model onboarding (first 2–3 releases)
  - Kernel changes / new CUDA/cuDNN versions
  - Unexpected regression in latency or throughput
  - Customer reports of degradation or cost increase

Tools and metrics:
  - perf suite (internal): runs unit microbenchmarks across kernels and sequence lengths.
  - nvprof / Nsight Systems: kernel-level timeline and occupancy analysis.
  - CUPTI / nsys: collect per-kernel durations and memcopy times.
  - Prometheus metrics: request_latency_ms (p50/p90/p99), tokens_per_second, batch_size_distribution, gpu_util_pct, gpu_mem_used_bytes, kernel_latency_{name}_ms.
  - Traces: OpenTelemetry request traces annotated with batching, scheduling decisions, and kernel selection.

Profiling workflow (numbered steps):
  1. Reproduce load pattern: use the benchmark harness (see section 4) to replay production-like traffic for the model and route.
  2. Collect high-level metrics: p50/p90/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, and batching stats from Prometheus for the run window.
  3. Attach Nsight/Profiler on an isolated worker and capture a 60–120s profile under steady-state load (prefer warm cache).
  4. Analyze hotspots: kernel durations, memcpy stalls, kernel launch overheads, and synchronization waits.
  5. Evaluate kernel variants: run perf suite across fp32/fp16/int8 and fused/unfused kernels; record token/sec and tail latency.
  6. Iterate: tune max_batch_size, queue budgets, and affinity. Re-run benchmark and compare metrics.

Example commands:
  - Run benchmark harness: ./bench/run_bench.sh --model llama-2-70b --seq 512 --qps 50 --duration 300 --route demo-pool
  - Start nsys capture: sudo nsys profile --output=profile.nsys --trace=cuda,nvtx ./inference-worker --model ...
  - Query Prometheus: sum(rate(tokens_generated_total[1m])) by (pool)

Minimum data to attach to tickets:
  - model name and version, pool config yaml, perf outputs (CSV), nsys/trace file, Prometheus time window, and representative input prompt if applicable.

4) Benchmarking suite

Benchmarks we run (automated in CI and nightly jobs):
  - Microbenchmarks: per-kernel single-request latency and memory footprint for 16/32/64/128-token runs.
  - Throughput benchmarks: sustained token/sec at varying sequence lengths (64/256/1024).
  - Tail-latency benchmarks: measure p99 under mixed QPS shapes and preemption events.
  - Cold-start benchmarks: model loading time and first-request latency.
  - Regression tests: compare new runtime builds against baseline commit.

How to run locally (quickstart):
  1. Checkout infra/bench repo and build the bench binary: make bench
  2. Start a single worker in dev mode: ./bin/inference-worker --model /models/llama-2-7b --dev
  3. Run bench: ./bench/bin/runner --target localhost:8080 --cases baseline,mix --duration 180

Example baseline expectations (Dedicated small class on A100-80GB):
  - single-request p50 (64 tokens): <= 30ms
  - single-request p99 (64 tokens): <= 120ms
  - tokens/sec sustained (seq=256, batch-mode): >= 1.2M tokens/minute (~20k tokens/sec)
  - model load time (cold): <= 18s

Regression detection and CI:
  - Nightly regression job compares token/sec and p99 for key models. Alerting rules kick a Jira ticket if degradation > 5% token/sec or > 10% p99. Attach full perf artifacts.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)

2026-12-10 — v4.18.0 (runtime):
  - Added fused attention kernel for LLaMA-family models; improves throughput by 22% for seq <=512.
  - Kernel selector now supports sequence-length buckets and proactive warmup.
  - Streaming improvements: per-token flush reduced by 40% latency in low-latency pools.
  - Bugfix: resolved rare deadlock in batcher when preemption is enabled.

2026-08-01 — v4.12.3 (runtime):
  - INT8 quantization pipeline stabilized; added safety checks to avoid hallucinations in QA-style prompts.
  - Updated Nsight capture scripts and added standard profiler markers.

6) Known issues & workarounds

Issue: occasional p99 spikes on mixed workloads when kernel selector caches stale kernel metadata
  - Symptoms: p99 increase by 2–3x for 10–30 minutes; affected pools show batcher backs up.
  - Root cause: metadata race updating kernel candidate list during rolling kernel rollout.
  - Workaround: restart affected worker(s) using ./tools/restart_worker.sh --id <id>; set pool kernel_policy to explicit ordering until rollout completes.

Issue: OOMs on A100-80 with fused kernels and large batch sizes
  - Symptoms: worker exits with CUDA OOM during sustained high-QPS with seq>1024.
  - Workaround: reduce max_batch_size for the pool to 1024 and enable memory-reserve flag in worker config.

Issue: degraded quality with aggressive INT8 in some QA prompts
  - Symptoms: model answers missing critical facts after switching to int8 kernels.
  - Workaround: set per-route kernel_policy to prefer fp16 for QA-heavy routes; run eval set to validate.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident response)

A. P99 latency regression (short-chat workloads)
  1. Verify alert: check Grafana dashboard and pager message.
  2. Determine scope: which pools and models affected (Prometheus label pool/model).
  3. Check batcher metrics: batch_size_distribution, queue_time_ms. If queue_time_ms > threshold, issue is batching backlog.
  4. If kernel_selector-related: inspect logs at /var/log/runtime/kernel_selector.log for recent rollouts. If rollout in progress, consider rolling back.
  5. Mitigation: set pool max_batch_size lower by 20% and increase priority weight for P0, or spin up additional worker nodes.
  6. Postmortem: capture traces, perf artifacts, and create incident ticket with steps taken and root cause.

B. Worker OOM / crash
  1. Collect worker logs and dmesg, and core dump if present.
  2. Check model and kernel_variant used by the worker; if fused kernels recently deployed, pin to previous commit.
  3. Restart worker and mark node draining in autoscaler until healthy.
  4. If reproducible, record exact repro steps and open a bug with kernel team.

C. KV cache miss storm causing cold-starts
  1. Inspect cache hit rate and evictions.
  2. If eviction rate is high, increase cache size for affected pool or adjust cache TTLs.
  3. For critical customers, enable prefill on rollout using prewarm job: ./tools/prefill_cache.sh --model <model> --pool <pool>.

Maintenance tasks (quarterly):
  - Review kernel selector heuristics and update sequence length buckets.
  - Run full perf sweep across top 10 customer models and compare to baseline.
  - Validate INT8 and quantization profiles against QA evaluation sets to detect regressions.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting commands
  - prometheus query sample: curl -g "http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le,pool))"
  - restart single worker: ./tools/restart_worker.sh --id <worker-id>
  - drain node: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl delete pod -l worker=<node> --grace-period=60
